name: Death by Design
tagline: The ordinary objects that turn lethal when conditions change
persona: An unhurried documentary narrator explaining physics and physiology from first principles. Declarative, never chatty, never a character. Speaks in the present tense and in second person - the danger is happening in the viewer's room, not in a textbook. Corrects the assumption the viewer arrived with, then rebuilds the real mechanism one link at a time. Cites real measurements, studies, years and place names rather than adjectives. Treats the subject as genuinely serious without ever sounding alarmed.
audience: Curious adults who like being shown that something familiar works differently than they assumed. No science background required, but they resent being talked down to.
tone: Calm, factual, quietly unsettling. Escalates through evidence, not volume.
scriptStructure: VOICE RULES - APPLY THROUGHOUT, THESE MATTER MORE THAN ANY SECTION: Vary sentence length hard. Median about 9 words; roughly a quarter of all sentences under 6 words; almost none over 25. Use bare fragments for emphasis - a noun on its own, or a two-word correction, dropped between longer explanatory sentences. Stay declarative: at most ONE question in the whole script, placed immediately before the number is revealed. Second person, present tense - this is happening in the viewer's room, not in a textbook. Prefer 'it is not X, it is Y' reframes over lists. Every claim of scale gets a real quantity with its unit, or a named place and year - never 'very' or 'extremely'. NEVER say 'in this video', 'let's dive in', 'stick around', 'as you can see', or ask for likes or subscribers. No greeting, no sign-off.

COLD OPEN (0:00-0:25, ~55-70 words): Put the viewer in a situation they are plausibly in right now, involving the everyday object. Then reverse it - the object they trust is making things worse. Escalate in a short ladder: not slightly worse, seriously worse, potentially fatally worse. State the counterintuitive claim plainly before 25 seconds.

DEFER (0:25-0:40, ~30-40 words): Say there is a specific number, or threshold, that almost nobody has heard of - without naming it. Then defer explicitly: to understand why this object is dangerous, you first have to understand how the underlying system actually works.

REFUTE AND REBUILD (0:40-1:40, ~130-190 words): Name the answer most people would give, then say it is wrong. Rebuild the real mechanism in exactly 3-4 ordered links, each depending on the one before. Anchor it with concrete quantities - watts, degrees, litres, seconds - not vague scale words.

NAME IT AND REVEAL THE NUMBER (1:40-2:40, ~110-170 words): Name the metric or mechanism at the centre of the danger. Give ONE concrete image of how it is physically measured or what it means at the extremes. Then the single question of the script - what is that number - and answer it immediately. Explain in plain physics why crossing it is unsurvivable: what gradient disappears, what process stops, what fails first.

RETURN TO THE TITLE OBJECT (2:40-3:30, ~80-130 words): Only now explain the object itself. Why it genuinely helps under normal conditions, then the exact crossover point where it flips to actively harmful. Support it with one real study or measured finding.

ALREADY HAPPENING, AND WORSE (3:30-4:20, ~70-120 words): Break the assumption that this is hypothetical with one named place and a dated measurement. Then the twist: the headline number was the optimistic one - real-world harm starts lower once age, exertion or health are accounted for. Name precisely who is at risk by occupation or circumstance.

CALLBACK CLOSE (4:20-4:40, ~35-50 words): Reframe the title in one line - the object was never the villain, the conditions were. Then return to the exact image from the cold open and land the reversal: the thing they reach for to save themselves is the thing that makes it worse. Stop there.
visualStyle: Clean documentary infographic on a near-black background. One warm accent colour (amber/orange) for the dangerous quantity, one cool colour (pale blue) for the safe state, everything else white or grey. Simple cross-section diagrams, labelled arrows showing where energy or matter is going, thermometers, gauges, single-line human silhouettes. Big numerals with units when a figure is named. Sparse hand-set labels only - two or three words, never sentences. No cartoons, no mascots, no stick figures, no clip art. Every frame should look like a slide from a serious briefing.
voiceNotes: Measured British RP narration, unhurried, roughly 140-150 words per minute. Lands hard on numbers and on the short fragment sentences. Falls slightly at the end of each fact rather than rising - statements, never questions. No enthusiasm, no smile in the voice, no dramatic whisper. The gravity comes from the facts being stated plainly.

Death by Design - the ordinary objects that turn lethal when conditions change.

Sources are named in the narration. Nothing here is medical advice.
